fetched_contents.title: IFRS - IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement
fetched_contents.text: IFRS 13 defines fair value, sets out a framework for measuring fair value, and requires disclosures about fair value measurements. It applies when another Standard requires or permits fair value measurements or disclosures about fair value measurements (and measurements based on fair value, such as fair value less costs to sell), except in specified circumstances in which other Standards govern. For example, IFRS 13 does not specify the measurement and disclosure requirements for share-based payment transactions, leases or impairment of assets. Nor does it establish disclosure requirements for fair values related to employee benefits and retirement plans. IFRS 13 defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date (an exit price). When measuring fair value, an entity uses the assumptions that market participants would use when pricing the asset or the liability under current market conditions, including assumptions about risk. As a result, an entity’s intention to hold an asset or to settle or otherwise fulfil a liability is not relevant when measuring fair value. In May 2011 the International Accounting Standards Board issued IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement. IFRS 13 defines fair value and replaces the requirement contained in individual Standards. Other Standards have made minor consequential amendments to IFRS 13. They include IAS 19 Employee Benefits (issued June 2011), Annual Improvements to IFRSs 2011–2013 Cycle (issued December 2013), IFRS 9 Financial Instruments (issued July 2014), IFRS 16 Leases (issued January 2016), IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements (issued April 2024) and IFRS 19 Subsidiaries without Public Accountability: Disclosures (issued in May 2024).

The extant literature shows that markets use a firm's accounting information to assess investment risk and that there is a high correlation between stock price volatility and earnings volatility (Beaver et al., 1970; Ryan, 1997). Reporting fair value adjustments in income is expected to increase transparency and to produce income figures that are closely aligned with underlying economic activity. However, the introduction of fair value accounting is expected to substantially increase the volatility of a firm's income (Barth et al., 1995; Hodder et al., 2006), and prior studies question whether this increased volatility facilitates investors' risk assessments (Ryan, 1997). 9 Difference-in-Differences – Causal Inference
The Mixtape Buy the print version today: \[ % Define terms \newcommand{\Card}{\text{Card }} \DeclareMathOperator*{\cov}{cov} \DeclareMathOperator*{\var}{var} \DeclareMathOperator{\Var}{Var\,} \DeclareMathOperator{\Cov}{Cov\,} \DeclareMathOperator{\Prob}{Prob} \newcommand{\independent}{\perp \!\!\! \perp} \DeclareMathOperator{\Post}{Post} \DeclareMathOperator{\Pre}{Pre} \DeclareMathOperator{\Mid}{\,\vert\,} \DeclareMathOperator{\post}{post} \DeclareMathOperator{\pre}{pre} \] The difference-in-differences design is an early quasi-experimental identification strategy for estimating causal effects that predates the randomized experiment by roughly eighty-five years. It has become the single most popular research design in the quantitative social sciences, and as such, it merits careful study by researchers everywhere.1 In this chapter, I will explain this popular and important research design both in its simplest form, where a group of units is treated at the same time, and the more common form, where groups of units are treated at different points in time. My focus will be on the identifying assumptions needed for estimating treatment effects, including several practical tests and robustness exercises commonly performed, and I will point you to some of the work on difference-in-differences design (DD) being done at the frontier of research. I have included several replication exercises as well. John Snow’s Cholera Hypothesis When thinking about situations in which a difference-in-differences design can be used, one usually tries to find an instance where a consequential treatment was given to some people or units but denied to others “haphazardly.” This is sometimes called a “natural experiment” because it is based on naturally occurring variation in some treatment variable that affects only some units over time. All good difference-in-differences designs are based on some kind of natural experiment. And one of the most interesting natural experiments was also one of the first difference-in-differences designs. This is the story of how John Snow convinced the world that cholera was transmitted by water, not air, using an ingenious natural experiment (Snow 1855). Cholera is a vicious disease that attacks victims suddenly, with acute symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea. In the nineteenth century, it was usually fatal. There were three main epidemics that hit London, and like a tornado, they cut a path of devastation through the city. Snow, a physician, watched as tens of thousands suffered and died from a mysterious plague. Doctors could not help the victims because they were mistaken about the mechanism that caused cholera to spread between people. The majority medical opinion about cholera transmission at that time was miasma, which said diseases were spread by microscopic poisonous particles that infected people by floating through the air. These particles were thought to be inanimate, and because microscopes at that time had incredibly poor resolution, it would be years before microorganisms would be seen. Treatments, therefore, tended to be designed to stop poisonous dirt from spreading through the air. But tried and true methods like quarantining the sick were strangely ineffective at slowing down this plague. John Snow worked in London during these epidemics. Originally, Snow—like everyone—accepted the miasma theory and tried many ingenious approaches based on the theory to block these airborne poisons from reaching other people. He went so far as to cover the sick with burlap bags, for instance, but the disease still spread. People kept getting sick and dying. Faced with the theory’s failure to explain cholera, he did what good scientists do—he changed his mind and began look for a new explanation. Snow developed a novel theory about cholera in which the active agent was not an inanimate particle but was rather a living organism. This microorganism entered the body through food and drink, flowed through the alimentary canal where it multiplied and generated a poison that caused the body to expel water. With each evacuation, the organism passed out of the body and, importantly, flowed into England’s water supply. People unknowingly drank contaminated water from the Thames River, which caused them to contract cholera. As they did, they would evacuate with vomit and diarrhea, which would flow into the water supply again and again, leading to new infections across the city. This process repeated through a multiplier effect which was why cholera would hit the city in epidemic waves. Snow’s years of observing the clinical course of the disease led him to question the usefulness of miasma to explain cholera. While these were what we would call “anecdote,” the numerous observations and imperfect studies nonetheless shaped his thinking. Here’s just a few of the observations which puzzled him. He noticed that cholera transmission tended to follow human commerce. A sailor on a ship from a cholera-free country who arrived at a cholera-stricken port would only get sick after landing or taking on supplies; he would not get sick if he remained docked. Cholera hit the poorest communities worst, and those people were the very same people who lived in the most crowded housing with the worst hygiene. He might find two apartment buildings next to one another, one would be heavily hit with cholera, but strangely the other one wouldn’t. He then noticed that the first building would be contaminated by runoff from privies but the water supply in the second building was cleaner. While these observations weren’t impossible to reconcile with miasma, they were definitely unusual and didn’t seem obviously consistent with miasmis. Snow tucked away more and more anecdotal evidence like these. But, while this evidence raised some doubts in his mind, he was not convinced. He needed a smoking gun…

Empirical evidence on the effects of specific IFRS fair value rules is shaped by the standards themselves and by studies that examine how firms report and disclose fair value under those rules. On IFRS 13, the evidence suggests that fair value measurement is not only a reporting requirement but also a disclosure requirement, with IFRS 13 defining fair value and requiring disclosures about fair value measurements. The standard applies when other standards require or permit fair value measurements or disclosures, and it establishes an exit-price framework for fair value, requiring entities to use assumptions market participants would use under current conditions rather than their own intentions [N2-F1]. This makes IFRS 13 a central standard for empirical work because it structures the measurement and disclosure environment that researchers can observe.

For IFRS 9, the evidence points to a more specific fair value context: financial instruments are classified and measured under IFRS 9, and the standard includes initial measurement at fair value plus or minus, depending on the classification. IFRS 9 also defines the measurement of financial assets and liabilities, and the literature indicates that IFRS 13 provides a consistent framework for measuring fair value across standards, including financial instruments [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-R5]. Empirical studies on IFRS 9 thus often focus on the impact of classification and measurement choices on financial instruments, including the distinction between amortized cost, fair value through other comprehensive income, and fair value through profit or loss. The evidence in the provided search material does not give a detailed empirical result for IFRS 9 itself, but it does establish that fair value under IFRS 9 is tied to the broader IFRS 13 measurement framework and that policy changes around fair value accounting are a plausible topic for empirical study [N2-F1] [N2-R5].

For IFRS 15, the evidence in the provided search material is more indirect. IFRS 15 concerns revenue recognition and does not directly require fair value measurement for revenue itself, but it may affect fair value-linked contracts. The search result for IFRS 15 revenue recognition indicates that the standard is relevant to fair value accounting in the broader IFRS system, and the search result on biological assets under IAS 41 implies that fair value measurement can also apply to contracts or assets outside a business combination [N2-R1] [N2-R3] [N2-R4] [N2-R5]. The broader evidence suggests that fair value-linked contracts and revenue recognition can interact, but the provided material does not present a direct empirical result for IFRS 15’s fair value effects. The industry-specific evidence is therefore thin here, and the best-supported conclusion is that IFRS 15 is part of the fair value measurement ecosystem rather than a standalone source of empirical findings in the provided evidence [N2-R1] [N2-R5].

Industry-specific differences are also evident. The search material includes studies on investment trusts, real estate, and long-lived operating assets, as well as biological assets and tangible assets. For example, the evidence on investment trusts shows that fair value earnings can affect stock price volatility, while the evidence on real estate suggests that firms may adopt fair value measurement for investment property before required changes and that such adoption can affect comparability and policy choice [N7-R2] [N7-R4]. The search on long-lived operating assets indicates that fair value measurement is studied as a useful or not useful practice for financial reporting [N4-R2]. The search on tangible assets and market perceptions also suggests that fair value reporting for tangible assets can be assessed by examining equity market reactions and event-related perceptions [N4-R5]. Overall, the empirical evidence supports a view that fair value outcomes vary across asset classes and industries, with real estate, investment trusts, and long-lived operating assets being particularly common subjects of study [N4-R2] [N4-R5] [N7-R2].

A limitation of the evidence provided is that it is largely descriptive and methodologically heterogeneous. The search results give titles and excerpts, but they do not provide full empirical results for each standard. So while IFRS 13, IFRS 9, and IFRS 15 are clearly relevant to fair value accounting research, the provided evidence does not allow a detailed synthesis of every empirical result. It does, however, support a strong conclusion that the effects of specific IFRS fair value rules are best understood through studies that combine standard-based measurement, disclosure, and industry-specific implementation differences [N2-F1] [N2-R5] [N4-R2] [N4-R5] [N7-R2].

Researchers measure fair value measurement outcomes through a combination of reported fair value changes, disclosures, earnings changes, market responses, equity volatility, and accounting quality indicators. The evidence shows that fair value accounting is often studied using event studies, regression analysis, and disclosure-focused methods. One key empirical paper in the provided material examines fair value accounting and issues with its implementation on the volatility of stock prices, reporting that stock price volatility is higher than the volatility of fair value earnings components and that this effect is driven partly by lack of accuracy in fair value estimates and a mismatch between fair value assets and historical-cost liabilities [N3-F2]. This is directly relevant to measuring changes in reported fair value and related disclosures, because it treats fair value earnings and their volatility as reported outcomes and links them to market reactions.

Changes in reported fair value and related disclosures are therefore a primary dependent variable in fair value research. The IFRS 13 evidence emphasizes that the standard requires disclosures about fair value measurements, so researchers can study whether firms change the amount, frequency, or detail of fair value disclosures when they adopt or modify fair value rules [N2-F1]. The broader fair value literature also suggests that researchers observe changes in fair value-linked assets and liabilities, including unrealized gains and losses, because those are directly affected by fair value measurement [N3-F2]. The evidence on tangible assets and market perceptions indicates that researchers also examine how firms report fair value for tangible assets and how investors interpret those reports [N4-R5].

Changes in earnings, income smoothing, and profitability are another major outcome class. The provided material shows that fair value earnings can be more volatile than historical-cost earnings, and that fair value accounting is often evaluated for its effect on earnings volatility and, by extension, on earnings informativeness [N3-F2]. The search result on fair value accounting and earnings volatility explicitly states that fair value-based earnings are more volatile than historical cost earnings, and it links that volatility to market responses and investor risk assessment [N3-R4]. The evidence also suggests that fair value can influence income smoothing or profitability indirectly, because earnings volatility affects how investors and analysts interpret a firm’s economic performance. In the investment trust study, the authors find that fair value earnings lead to greater stock price volatility, which is economically meaningful because it suggests that fair value changes can distort market perceptions of a firm’s underlying economic condition [N3-F2].

Changes in market responses and equity volatility are a central part of the empirical agenda. The provided evidence repeatedly connects fair value accounting to stock price volatility and abnormal returns. One paper examines stock returns of financial institutions following the adoption of fair value option for liabilities during the financial crisis, showing that policy changes can trigger market responses [N3-R2]. The investment trust paper reports that stock price volatility is higher than the volatility of fair value earnings components, and it attributes this to unrealized fair value earnings and implementation issues [N3-F2]. The broader market-perception literature on tangible assets also suggests that equity market reactions can be measured through abnormal volatility and trading volume [N3-R5]. These findings indicate that researchers use cumulative abnormal returns, market volatility, and trading activity as key dependent variables to assess fair value effects on market reactions [N3-R2] [N3-R5] [N3-F2].

Changes in accounting conservatism and information content are implied but less directly documented in the provided evidence. The investment trust paper argues that fair value accounting is expected to increase transparency and align income with underlying economic activity, which supports the view that fair value should improve information content [N3-F2]. It also notes that regulators are concerned fair value can make firms appear more volatile than they actually are, which implies a concern about conservatism or the accuracy of reported earnings [N3-F2]. The evidence on disclosure requirements under IFRS 13 further supports the idea that fair value measurement affects the informativeness of financial statements through more detailed reporting [N2-F1]. While the provided material does not give a direct empirical decomposition of conservatism, it does suggest that researchers infer accounting quality from volatility, transparency, and market responses [N3-F2] [N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence shows that researchers measure fair value effects through a broad set of outcomes: reported fair value and disclosures, earnings volatility and profitability, market responses and equity volatility, and inferred accounting quality. The most consistent pattern is that fair value changes are studied as both accounting outcomes and market signals, with volatility and abnormal returns serving as major indicators of economic relevance [N3-F2] [N3-R2] [N3-R5] [N2-F1].

Researchers interpret and critique empirical findings on fair value accounting by assessing robustness, distinguishing statistically significant from economically meaningful effects, and identifying limitations such as reverse causality and omitted variables. The evidence in the provided material shows that robustness is a major concern. One study on fair value accounting and earnings volatility reports that fair value earnings lead to greater stock price volatility when investment trust shares are traded by unsophisticated investors and are followed by fewer analysts, which suggests that findings are sensitive to sample characteristics [N3-F2]. Another paper on fair value and stock returns during the financial crisis focuses on stock returns of financial institutions following adoption of the fair value option for liabilities, indicating that researchers often test findings across different treatment or policy-change settings [N3-R2]. These examples support the idea that researchers test findings across specifications, samples, and settings to ensure robustness [N3-F2] [N3-R2].

Economically meaningful versus statistically significant effects are also a key interpretation issue. The investment trust study finds that stock price volatility is higher than the volatility of fair value earnings components, and it attributes this effect to an unrealized fair value component and implementation issues [N3-F2]. That is an economically meaningful result because it suggests that fair value changes can have real market consequences, even if the effect is not purely a direct earnings effect. The paper also notes that fair value earnings are more volatile than historical cost earnings, which is economically meaningful because it affects investor risk assessments and market perceptions [N3-R4]. In contrast, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of effect sizes across studies, so the clearest takeaway is that researchers interpret fair value studies as evidence of both statistical significance and economic significance, with market volatility and investor sophistication often serving as the main interpreters of economic meaning [N3-F2] [N3-R4].

Limitations such as reverse causality and omitted variables are a recurring concern. The provided evidence on endogeneity and controls indicates that omitted variable bias is a well-known problem in accounting research, and that failure to include confounding controls can bias results [N6-R2]. The evidence also highlights reverse causality as one of the main sources of endogeneity, with the ScienceDirect entry noting that endogeneity problems arise when errors are not random, making it difficult to identify causal effects [N6-R1]. The Kothari/Warner evidence on event studies further suggests that researchers are concerned with the statistical properties of event-study methods and with identification, which is directly relevant to reverse causality and other identification issues [N5-F4]. In the fair value context, these limitations are especially important because firms may adopt fair value policies for reasons other than pure measurement change, and market responses may reflect broader shocks rather than the fair value rule itself [N3-R2] [N6-R1] [N6-R2].

The evidence also implies that researchers recognize policy and practice implications. The investment trust paper notes that fair value accounting can make firms appear more volatile than they actually are, which is a concern for regulators and suggests a policy implication about the credibility of financial reporting [N3-F2]. The evidence on IFRS adoption and policy changes indicates that researchers study the consequences of IFRS adoption, including how firms choose accounting policies and whether fair value adoption affects comparability or information asymmetry [N7-R1] [N7-R4]. The broader IFRS literature also suggests that researchers consider the political economy and market outcomes of international accounting standards, implying that empirical findings are often interpreted in terms of reporting practices, transparency, and regulatory influence [N7-R3]. These implications show that researchers do not merely report statistical findings; they also assess whether the findings matter for accounting practice, disclosure quality, and regulatory design [N7-R1] [N7-R4] [N7-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation of fair value accounting studies. Researchers use robustness tests across specifications and samples, distinguish statistically significant from economically meaningful effects, and repeatedly point to reverse causality and omitted variables as major threats to identification. At the same time, they emphasize policy and practice implications because fair value effects are often tied to transparency, volatility, and regulatory concern [N3-F2] [N3-R2] [N6-R1] [N6-R2] [N7-R1] [N7-R4].

The evidence in the provided material shows that event studies are a common design. One search result describes event studies as examining the impact of identifiable events on variables of economic interest, and another describes them as the oldest and simplest causal inference research design that predates experiments and statistics [N1-R1] [N1-R3]. A related source on event studies in economics and finance states that they examine the behavior of firms' stock prices around corporate events, further supporting their use as a causal inference method [N1-R4]. Event studies are especially useful when researchers want to isolate the effect of a fair value-related policy change, such as a fair value option adoption or an IFRS adoption, because they can compare outcomes before and after the event [N1-R1] [N1-R3].

Difference-in-differences (DID) is another major identification strategy. The provided evidence explains that DID is a widely used causal inference method for estimating policy interventions or exogenous shocks when randomized experiments are not available, and that it is a quasi-experimental design based on natural variation in treatment [N5-R1] [N5-R2]. A practical guide to DID emphasizes that the design requires identifying assumptions, and that it is often used when treatment is applied at different times to different groups [N5-F4]. In the fair value context, DID is useful for comparing firms or industries that adopted fair value rules at different times or under different conditions, allowing researchers to separate the effect of the fair value change from other time trends [N5-R1] [N5-R2].

The evidence also supports the use of more general causal inference methods. The search result on robust methods in event studies notes that researchers can measure cumulative abnormal returns and changes in systematic risk, such as beta, associated with events [N1-R2]. This indicates that researchers do not rely only on simple event-study methods but also incorporate risk-adjusted measures and robustness checks. The broader causal inference literature in the search results reinforces the idea that fair value studies often seek to identify treatment effects using quasi-experimental designs rather than purely observational ones [N1-R5] [N5-R1] [N5-R2].

The fair value option for liabilities literature also shows that policy changes, such as adoption of the fair value option, can trigger market responses and affect stock returns [N3-R2]. The evidence further suggests that IFRS adoption and policy changes are often treated as exogenous shocks, which is why they are suitable for causal identification [N7-R1] [N7-R4]. In short, researchers typically use IFRS adoption, fair value policy changes, or other treatment events as the triggering mechanism in fair value studies [N7-R1] [N7-R4] [N3-R2].

Dependent variables used to measure effects include earnings, volatility, and market responses. The provided evidence repeatedly uses earnings volatility and stock price volatility as outcomes. One study finds that fair value earnings are more volatile than historical cost earnings, and that stock price volatility is higher than the volatility of fair value earnings components [N3-R4] [N3-F2]. Another study on fair value option for liabilities reports stock returns of financial institutions following adoption, showing that market responses are a central dependent variable [N3-R2]. The evidence on event studies also shows that researchers measure cumulative abnormal returns and beta changes, indicating that market responses are treated as key outcomes [N1-R2] [N1-R4]. These findings support the conclusion that earnings volatility, stock price volatility, and market responses are the most commonly measured outcomes in fair value accounting studies [N3-R4] [N3-F2] [N1-R2] [N1-R4].

Researchers address endogeneity and measurement error through several strategies. The endogeneity literature in the provided evidence notes that endogeneity problems arise when errors are not random, making it difficult to identify causal effects [N6-R1]. It also emphasizes omitted variable bias as a major concern, and highlights that failure to include confounding controls can introduce bias [N6-R2]. The evidence on reverse causality and omitted variables further supports the idea that researchers must control for confounding factors and consider reverse causality when interpreting results [N6-R1] [N6-R2]. In practice, researchers often use robustness tests across specifications and samples, as well as quasi-experimental designs such as DID and event studies, to strengthen identification [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that researchers pay attention to measurement error, because fair value estimates can be inaccurate and can create artificial volatility due to mismatched assets and liabilities [N3-F2]. Taken together, the evidence shows that fair value studies are designed with a strong identification focus, using event studies, DID, and robustness checks to address endogeneity and measurement error [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-F4] [N6-R1] [N6-R2] [N3-F2].

Researchers empirically investigate the effects of IFRS fair value accounting rules by combining accounting-standard analysis, empirical measurement, and causal identification. The evidence shows that fair value studies are not a single methodological template, but a family of approaches that vary by research design, dependent variable, treatment trigger, and the specific IFRS standard being studied [N1-R1] [N2-F1] [N2-R1] [N7-R1] [N7-R4]. Below is a synthesized account of how they do this.

## 1) How researchers design empirical studies of fair value accounting effects
Researchers typically choose among several research designs and identification strategies. Event studies are a common starting point because they examine the impact of identifiable events on economic outcomes and are described as the oldest and simplest causal inference design [N1-R1] [N1-R3]. Event studies are especially useful when the fair value-related policy change is exogenous, such as the adoption of a fair value option or an IFRS adoption [N3-R2] [N7-R1] [N7-R4]. They are also used to measure cumulative abnormal returns and changes in systematic risk, including beta, associated with events [N1-R2] [N1-R4].

Difference-in-differences (DID) is another major identification strategy. DID is a quasi-experimental design used when randomized experiments are not available, and it is especially useful for comparing treatment and control groups or for comparing treatment at different times [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-F4]. This makes it well suited for IFRS adoption or policy-change studies, where researchers can estimate the effect of fair value measurement by comparing firms or industries that adopted the policy with those that did not [N7-R1] [N7-R4].

More generally, the evidence indicates that fair value studies often rely on causal inference methods rather than purely observational analysis. The broader causal inference literature in the branch reports reinforces the use of identification strategies to separate fair value effects from other time trends or confounding factors [N1-R5] [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-F4]. This is important because fair value changes are often difficult to isolate in the real world.

## 2) The dependent variables used to measure effects
Researchers measure the effects of fair value accounting through a broad set of outcomes. The most commonly used are **earnings volatility**, **market responses**, and **equity volatility**.
